1. Before Writing
2. Marks That Meant Something
3. Pictures Become Words
4. The Great Invention: The Alphabet
5. Writing in Africa
6. Making Books for Everyone
7. Writing Today

cuneiform: the oldest known writing, wedge marks pressed in clay
hieroglyphs: Egyptian writing made of small pictures
alphabet: a set of letters that stand for sounds
Nsibidi: an ancient Nigerian system of symbols
manuscript: a book written by hand
printing press: a machine that stamps pages of words

Imagine a world with no writing at all. No books, no letters, no signs, no messages on a screen. Everything anyone knew had to be held in their head or spoken aloud. When an old person died, all the stories and knowledge inside them could die too. For most of human history, this was how it was.

image.note: An elder telling stories to children round a fire at night; nothing written anywhere; warm, oral

pages.text: People passed knowledge on by speaking, singing and remembering. Griots in West Africa could recite the history of whole kingdoms from memory. It worked, but it was fragile. A story is only as safe as the last person who remembers it. People needed a way to make thoughts last longer than a life.

image.note: A West African griot with a kora, a crowd listening; respected, skilled

pages.text: The first step was small. People began to make marks to keep count. A farmer might cut notches on a stick, one for each goat. A trader might press small clay tokens to record a deal. These marks were not yet writing, but they were the seed of it: a mark on the world that stood for an idea.

image.note: A clay tablet with counting marks and small tokens beside it; ancient, simple

pages.text: About five thousand years ago, in the land between two great rivers called Mesopotamia, this idea grew up. People pressed a reed into wet clay to make wedge-shaped marks. We call it cuneiform, and it is the oldest writing we know. At first it recorded sacks of grain. Soon it recorded laws, letters and even poems.

image.note: A scribe pressing a reed stylus into a wet clay tablet, wedge marks forming; concentrated

pages.text: Far away in Egypt, along the River Nile, people invented a different kind of writing. They drew tiny pictures called hieroglyphs: an owl, a hand, a wave of water. Some pictures stood for things, and some stood for sounds. A wall covered in hieroglyphs is beautiful, but it took years to learn to read.

image.note: A temple wall covered in colourful Egyptian hieroglyphs; a scribe pointing; rich, detailed

pages.text: In China, writing grew from pictures too, and it never stopped. Chinese characters began as little drawings of things, then became the elegant symbols still used by more than a billion people today. It is one of the oldest writing systems on Earth that is still in daily use. Some marks made long ago never went away.

image.note: A brush painting a Chinese character on paper; ancient bone script shown beside a modern character

pages.text: All these systems had a problem. They needed hundreds, even thousands, of different signs. Learning to write took most of a childhood, so only a few people, usually priests and officials, ever could. Writing was power, and that power was locked up tight.

image.note: A tired young trainee scribe surrounded by hundreds of symbols on scrolls; overwhelmed

pages.text: Then, around the eastern shore of the sea, a clever people called the Phoenicians had a brilliant idea. Instead of a sign for every word, why not a sign for every sound? With only a couple of dozen marks, you could spell anything you could say. This was the alphabet, and it changed the world.

image.note: Phoenician traders on a ship, a short row of simple letter-marks on a scroll; light dawning

pages.text: The idea spread like fire. The Greeks borrowed it and added letters for vowels. The Romans borrowed it from the Greeks and shaped the letters you are reading right now. The very letters on this page travelled thousands of years and thousands of miles to reach you. Every one is a tiny inheritance.

image.note: A row showing a letter changing shape: Phoenician to Greek to Roman A; a timeline arrow

pages.text: Africa has its own proud writing stories, often left out of the books. In south-eastern Nigeria, the Igbo people used a system of symbols called Nsibidi, some of them so secret that only certain people could read them. They were carved, painted and even danced. Nsibidi is Nigeria's own ancient writing.

image.note: Nsibidi symbols carved on a wooden panel and painted on cloth; a Nigerian elder explaining; proud

pages.text: To the north, Africa wrote in Arabic script. In the city of Timbuktu, in Mali, scholars filled great libraries with thousands of handwritten books on law, medicine and the stars. While some people far away imagined Africa had no writing, Timbuktu held libraries older than many in Europe.

image.note: A Timbuktu scholar handling old manuscripts in a mudbrick library; shelves of books; dignified

pages.text: And in the mountains of Ethiopia, people wrote in their own script, called Geez, which is still used in churches today. Africa was never a place without writing. It was, and is, a place with many writings, each one carrying the mind of a people across time.

image.note: An Ethiopian priest reading a hand-lettered Geez book; incense, warm light

pages.text: For a long time, every book had to be copied out by hand, one word at a time. A single book could take a person a whole year to make, so books were rare and costly. Only the rich and the powerful owned them. Knowledge stayed locked up.

image.note: A monk copying a book by hand by candlelight; slow, painstaking

pages.text: Then, about five hundred years ago, came a machine that changed everything: the printing press. It could stamp a whole page of words at once, again and again. Suddenly one book could become a thousand books. Prices fell. Ordinary people, for the first time, could own books and learn to read them.

image.note: An early printing press, sheets of freshly printed pages hanging to dry; excitement

pages.text: The story did not stop. Writing moved from clay to paper, from paper to screens. Now you can write a message in Abuja and someone reads it in Lagos a second later. The same invention that began with a farmer counting goats now carries billions of words around the world every day.

image.note: A modern Nigerian child typing on a phone, a speech bubble of letters flowing to another child far away

pages.text: Think about what writing really is. It lets a person who lived thousands of years ago speak to you today. It lets you send your thoughts to someone you will never meet. Every time you read a word, you are using one of the greatest inventions humans ever made. And now, you can use it too.

image.note: A child writing in a notebook, the words lifting off the page as glowing letters; hopeful, closing
